title: Warmup and microburst latency sweep across SKUs
content:
Quick note: this is a working doc capturing microburst/warmup characteristics observed while benchmarking token-level and short-sequence latencies across a range of cloud SKUs and driver/CUDA combinations. Aim is to surface actionable mitigations (runtime settings, kernel choices, placement policies) rather than a full polished report.

Context and motivation:
- Several customer reports and internal alerts show occasional 2-5x spikes on 1-2% of regeneration requests even when mean latency is stable.
- Existing perf docs target throughput and occupancy (longer sequences, steady-state). We suspected warmup, kernel load jitter, and host <-> device interactions (PCIe, NVLINK, driver housekeeping) as root causes for these microbursts.
- This sweep intentionally focuses on short inference shapes (<= 64 tokens) and single-request scenarios that are latency-sensitive for chat UX.

Hypotheses under test:
1) Cold kernel dispatches and CUDA context management cause a significant fraction of tail latency for short requests.
2) Specific driver/CUDA pairs produce sporadic background defragmentation/housekeeping work that shows up as microbursts.
3) Instance SKUs with different PCIe/host configurations (and MIG behavior) show different tail behavior even at similar median latencies.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- GPUs: A100 (40GB and 80GB), H100 (80GB), L40S (48GB)
- Cloud SKUs: gcp-a2-highgpu-1g, aws-p4d, aws-p5, azure-nvads (representative names, mapped to internal sku ids)
- Drivers/CUDA: driver-525.85 / CUDA 11.8, driver-535.54 / CUDA 12.2, driver-545.x / CUDA 12.3 (H100 optimized builds)
- Runtime config: small-batch=1, batching disabled, batching= enabled with max_batch_size=8 (to see batching impact on warmup), kernel-cache enabled/disabled, prefix-kv cache warm/unwarm
- Workloads: short prompt (8 tokens), medium prompt (32 tokens), burst of 10 sequential single-token requests (simulate keystroke streaming)
- Metric surface: p50, p95, p99, p999 latencies (token generation), percentage of requests > 2x median, kernel load time, context-switch time (host), PCIe stats (when available), GPU SM activity spikes

Measurement methodology notes:
- Tests run on dedicated instances to avoid noisy-neighbor interference. For each config: 10k single-request samples (randomized inter-arrival 50-150ms) + 100 bursts of 10x requests at 10RPS.
- Used our tracing hook to emit event markers at: request enqueue, kernel launch, first token produced, token complete.
- Where possible captured nvidia-smi sampling and driver logs to correlate ephemeral spikes with driver messages.
- All runs after a fresh reboot and with a warmup period of 100 dummy requests for steady-state comparison. An explicit cold-start series was also run (no warmup).

Key findings (summary):
- Mean latencies are broadly similar across SKUs for short requests (within ~10%). But tail behavior diverges: H100 instances show better p95/p99 by ~15% versus A100 in driver 525 series, but when upgrading to driver 545.x H100 shows further tail improvement.
- Cold-start (no warmup) penalty is large for token-1 latency on all GPUs: ~1.8-3.0x median depending on driver. This is driven by kernel module load and CUDA context creation.
- Microbursts (isolated spikes) correlated often with driver-side housekeeping messages in syslog (periodic buffer reclamation and page migration on some instances). These were more frequent on older driver/CUDA combos on specific cloud SKUs.
- PCIe-constrained SKUs (host with PCIe Gen3 vs Gen4 differences) had higher variance in the first token latency, presumably due to larger host->device transfer jitter for small control packets.
- Batch coalescing disabled (single) has lower median but higher p99 in some SKUs. Enabling small batching (max_batch=4) reduced p99 for medium workloads because it amortizes per-request overhead. For keystroke-like bursts, batching introduces added jitter if burst timing is irregular.
- KV-cache cold misses amplify warmup tails: when model needs to populate KV cache across many layers for the first streaming tokens, kernel launch spikes are higher. Pre-warming KV-cache reduced p99 by up to 30% on A100.

Representative numbers (selected):
- A100, driver-525, single-request, 8-token: p50=18ms, p95=32ms, p99=72ms, p999=160ms; cold-start first-token median=41ms
- H100, driver-545, single-request, 8-token: p50=15ms, p95=26ms, p99=54ms, p999=110ms; cold-start first-token median=28ms
- L40S, driver-535, single-request, 8-token: p50=16ms, p95=34ms, p99=90ms, p999=220ms; observed occasional 500ms outliers tied to host I/O noise

Interesting anomalies we followed up on:
- On one AWS SKU we saw repeated ~200ms microbursts every ~7 minutes. Driver logs showed periodic GPU health telemetry flushes (nv-hostengine) triggered by host monitoring agent. Disabling the host agent eliminated the pattern. We should add a telemetry check in our instance profile for Dedicated instances.
- On Azure L40S the first-token latency had a bimodal distribution. Investigation pointed to inconsistent NUMA placement of the inference process and the device DMA region. Pinning process to correct NUMA node eliminated bimodality.

Immediate mitigations recommended (practical):
- Always perform a lightweight KV-cache warmup for chat sessions: send an empty or short prompt prefetch on session start to reduce cold tails. Add to SDK quickstart.
- Default to small coalescing window (e.g., 5ms) with max_batch_size=4 for public hosted latency-sensitive routes. Provide per-route override.
- Add driver/telemetry sanity checks to Dedicated deployment templates: detect and warn if host monitoring agents are flushing nv-hostengine on schedule.
- For Private/on-prem: document NUMA affinity and recommend pinned deployment layouts for L40S-class devices.

Longer-term actions and experiments:
- Work with compiler/runtime team to reduce kernel dispatch overhead for trivial kernels (micro-op fusion, persistent kernels for short sequences). This is likely the best path to reduce cold-start token-1 cost.
- Investigate kernel-level preloader at agent boot that performs minimal context init so first user request is mostly free. We need to weigh memory/latency tradeoffs.
- Formalize a microburst detection alert in Console: surface p99/p999 spikes at route level and correlate with recent driver/instance metadata.
- Run similar sweep under multi-tenant stress to measure whether microbursts amplify under noisy neighbors (next sprint).

Open questions / things to verify:
- Does the cloud provider's hypervisor or host agent trigger driver housekeeping differently across regions? We saw region-skewed patterns for a particular SKU. Need provider-side confirmation.
- How do persistent kernels interact with model quantization paths? Some quantized kernels look to take longer to JIT in older drivers.
- Can we reliably predict which SKUs will benefit from pre-warm vs batching? Need an automated heuristic in the router.

Raw artifacts location and short runbook:
- Raw trace bundles: gs://redwood-test-artifacts/warmup-sweep/2025-09-03/*.tgz
- Snippets + flamegraphs: gs://redwood-test-artifacts/warmup-sweep/2025-09-03/flamegraphs
- To reproduce: checkout serving-runtime branch warmup-microburst-sweep, run scripts/bench/warmup_sweep.sh --sku <sku> --driver <driver> --warmup=0|100 --samples=10000

Next steps for this doc:
- Marco to add full p95/p99 tables for all runs (in progress).
- Leah to file infra request to add a host-agent check in Dedicated AMI images.
- Omar to prototype a tiny persistent-kernel preloader and measure memory cost.
- Nina to draft a small SDK change to do optional KV-cache prewarm on session open.

Notes-to-self: capture one short video showing the bimodal NUMA effect with and without pinning; that helped the infra team accept the change quicker before.

If reviewers want, I can convert this to a short Confluence page with simplified graphs and an executive summary. For now keeping it in Drive so we can iterate quickly.

-- Asha
